title: Thinking as a Sikh today

lines: A PHONE, A MACHINE, A WARMING PLANET.
THE GRANTH NEVER MENTIONS A SCREEN.
AN OLD BOOK, A NEW WORLD.
cards: What would the Gurus say about a phone that never stops buzzing? About a machine that can write a hymn? About medicine that can keep a body breathing long after the person seems gone?
About a planet getting warmer? None of these questions existed when the hymns were sung. The Granth never mentions a screen.

And yet Sikhs carry these questions into the gurdwara all the same, right past the shoes left at the door. So how do you think with an old book about a new world, without pretending it says what it doesn't?

teach.b: First, the Granth asks for thinking. In Raag Asa, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that when learning is truly reflected on, a person becomes a help to others.
The word is vichar: reflection, turning a teaching over until it's yours. Reading isn't the end; thinking it through is part of the practice. Second, a daily habit.
Each day in the gurdwara, the Granth is opened and a hymn read from where it opens.

teach.h: THE HUKAMNAMA: AN ORDER EACH DAY.
teach.b: That reading is the hukamnama, the order of the day. Sikhs bring whatever they're carrying to it, and then sit with what comes back: an old Word speaking into a new morning.
Third, the community. When a new question touches the whole Sikh community, Sikh bodies such as the Akal Takht in Amritsar sometimes speak to it.
Sikhs also talk, write and sometimes disagree, in homes and gurdwaras and online. Thinking as a Sikh today is done in company.
Fourth, principle, not proof-text. There's no verse about phones. But there are threads you've met all year: remember the Name, work honestly, share, the Light in everyone, the good of all.
Hold a new question up to those, and it starts to sort itself. Does this tool help me remember, or only forget? Does this choice treat everyone as carrying the same Light?
Old word, new question, and the patience to let them meet.

how: Gurdwaras read a hukamnama, a hymn taken from where the Guru Granth Sahib opens, as the order of the day; Sikhs also discuss new questions together, and Sikh bodies such as the Akal Takht sometimes issue guidance.

games.q: what does “thinking as a sikh today” mean?
o: finding a verse that names each new invention
bringing new questions to old teachings, with care
setting old teachings aside for modern ones

games.q: thinking as a Sikh today: tap the pairs.
p: the order of the day from the Granth
a Sikh body that can speak to new questions
hold the question up to the threads

s: the Granth has a direct verse for every modern question
it never mentions a screen; Sikhs bring new questions to its principles.
each day the gurdwara takes a hymn from where the Granth opens
that reading is the hukamnama, the order of the day.
Guru Nanak says learning only matters if it's memorized
he says learning reflected on makes a person a help to others.

games.q: you're facing a modern choice the Gurus never wrote about. how does the lesson suggest you think it through?
o: decide the Granth has nothing to say.
hold it up to the threads: remembering, honest work, sharing, the good of all.
find any single line and treat it as the answer.
games.why: principle, not proof-text: vichar means turning the teaching over until it speaks to the new question.

practice: Let one real question come up, something the old world never faced, a choice about screens, money, work or a relative's care, and say it to yourself plainly.
Then hold it up to one thread per breath: remembering, honest work, sharing, the good of all. Notice which thread tugs, and stay with it.

wordCard.voice: Thinking as a Sikh today. Vichar, reflection, bringing new questions to the old Word, with the community and the day's hukamnama. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: vichar, reflection, thinking a teaching through.

carryVoice: Your line: old word, new questions. The Granth never mentions a screen, and it still has threads to hold. I'll be here tomorrow.
